tldr: To harvest lettuce in narrow hydroponic lanes without damaging crops, this paper develops "PSA-PPO," a reinforcement learning method that builds approach-path and tool-pose safety directly into the policy. It demonstrates zero-shot transfer from simulation-only training to a physical UR10e arm and highly reliable harvesting motions.
hero_caption: An overview of the proposed Sim-to-Real lettuce harvesting framework. The wrist-mounted camera (top) detects the lettuce cutting point, while the safe side-approach policy (PSA-PPO) trained in the simulator (Isaac Lab, bottom) is applied directly to the physical arm, safely harvesting even in obstacle-rich hydroponic beds.
overview:
Harvesting lettuce in greenhouse hydroponics (NFT system) is a demanding task for robotic arms. The robot must slip its cutting blade into the stem just millimeters above the ground at the correct angle, all while dodging densely packed soft leaves and surrounding cultivation rails. Conventional sampling-based motion planning (such as RRT) suffers from singularities, vibrations, and planning failures. On the other hand, letting standard reinforcement learning (RL) explore by trial and error on physical hardware is impossible due to severe collision risks.

The authors propose "PSA-PPO," which learns safe approach trajectories entirely from scratch in simulation (Isaac Lab) and transfers directly without real-world fine-tuning. The algorithm keeps the standard PPO objective intact, but cleverly combines geometric initialization, corridor-aware spatial constraints on the approach path, and reward shaping that tracks height-violation histories of the tool and wrist links. This allows the policy to acquire crop-proximal approach motions tailored for harvesting.

The authors conducted simulation ablation experiments, a 150-target physical benchmark on a UR10e against classical planners (RRTConnect, RRT*, Cartesian+TOTG), and a full greenhouse harvesting evaluation across 144 lettuce plants. In the physical benchmark, PSA-PPO achieved the highest reaching rate of 94.7% and substantially reduced jerk (a measure of motion smoothness). In the production greenhouse environment, it achieved an 86.1% complete harvesting success rate.
contributions: Proposal of PSA-PPO, a local reaching policy incorporating geometric constraints and approach-path safety history to learn side approaches in confined hydroponic setups
Demonstration of zero-shot Sim-to-Real transfer to a UR10e arm without real-world fine-tuning, trained entirely in Isaac Lab's massively parallel GPU simulation environment
Verification on a 150-target physical benchmark, achieving a 94.7% reaching rate that significantly outperforms classical planners while reducing jerk by 39.8–73.0%
Achievement of a 94.4% target-reaching rate and an 86.1% complete harvesting success rate in real greenhouse harvesting trials (144 attempts) integrating RGB-D vision and a cut-and-hold mechanism

sections.heading: Why Is the Harvesting Approach for Hydroponic Lettuce So Difficult?
sections.summary: Automated harvesting of hydroponic lettuce requires delivering the blade to the base of the stem at an accurate angle without colliding with crowded crops or cultivation rails. Conventional motion planning struggles with vibrations and singularities, while trial and error with standard RL is dangerous on real hardware. Simulation-only training solves this issue.
sections.details:
Robotic harvesting in protected horticulture is completely different from structured industrial settings. Crops vary in shape and softness, and nutrient film technique (NFT) gullies and neighboring leaves crowd the workspace. To harvest lettuce, the blade must slide horizontally into a tight space just above the ground without hitting any of these obstacles.

Sampling-based motion planners like RRT and BIT*, as well as Cartesian trajectory generators, excel at finding geometric paths. However, they are sensitive to singularities and computational noise, often producing abrupt joint reversals and unstable vibrations (high jerk). On the other hand, deep reinforcement learning (DRL) can yield smooth controllers adapted to environments, but letting a real robot collide repeatedly during trial-and-error exploration is not an option.

This makes physics simulators running in parallel on GPUs (such as NVIDIA Isaac Lab) an attractive alternative. Still, closing the sim-to-real reality gap and getting RL to satisfy strict, crop-specific geometric constraints—not just reaching the final goal, but entering from a specified horizontal orientation while maintaining height clearance—remain major hurdles. This paper tackles these challenges with PSA-PPO, tailoring the task design specifically for harvesting.

sections.heading: PSA-PPO: Training Safe Side Approaches Entirely in Simulation
sections.summary: Without altering the standard PPO formulation, PSA-PPO achieves safe entry by using target-conditioned safe initialization, virtual corridor tracking, and violation-history penalties for the wrist and tool. It also integrates RGB-D target tracking with temporal smoothing and a 3D-printed cut-and-hold mechanism.
sections.details:
### 2.1 3D Target Streaming
A wrist-mounted RGB-D camera detects the cutting point at the base of the lettuce. To suppress frame-to-frame depth noise, detected 2D positions are tracked, and 3D coordinates from recent frames are temporally averaged in a buffer and streamed as ROS topics.

### 2.2 PSA-PPO Training Formulation
The core idea of PSA-PPO is separating coarse positioning from long range and precise side-approach from close range. Once the target position $\mathbf{p}^T$ is determined, a standby point $\mathbf{p}^S$ horizontally shifted by $d_a$ and a horizontal approach vector $\mathbf{a}^T$ are automatically derived. The arm first moves to a geometrically safe start pose based on the target, and the policy (actor) controls only the final approach segment from there.

The actor receives a 42-dimensional observation including joint positions, velocities, position error to the target, tool-approach alignment, and vertical clearance information for the tool and wrist links. The reward function penalizes deviations from a virtual approach corridor, tool tilt, and the accumulated depth of violations whenever the tool or wrist dips below the safety baseline during the approach, in addition to rewarding progress toward the target. Final target reaching also requires that the arm never breached the safety plane throughout the entire trajectory (strict success criteria).

### 2.3 & 2.4 Physical Deployment and Harvesting Sequence
The end-effector uses a custom leverage-based "cut-and-hold mechanism" driven by an OnRobot 2FG7 electric gripper. A single grasping action cuts the stem and holds the plant simultaneously. When deploying the trained policy to the physical UR10e, no real-world fine-tuning is performed. Instead, deterministic inference issues joint commands at each step via fixed Cartesian offsets and a ROS joint trajectory controller. A safety limiter in the ROS layer prevents abrupt commands.

captions.F2: Architecture diagram of PSA-PPO training. Standby points and horizontal approach directions are geometrically calculated from the target. The policy outputs 6-DoF joint increment commands from 42-dimensional observations, including wrist and tool height clearances. Trajectory safety violation histories are incorporated into rewards and termination criteria.
captions.F3: The newly designed cut-and-hold harvesting end-effector. Linked to the opening and closing of the OnRobot 2FG7 gripper, it simultaneously cuts the stem with pruning shears and grasps the plant with holding fingers.

sections.heading: Physical Arm Shootout and Real Greenhouse Harvesting Tests
sections.summary: After validating the importance of path-safety rewards via simulation ablations, PSA-PPO was evaluated against three classical planners on a physical UR10e across 150 targets. PSA-PPO achieved the highest reaching rate (94.7%) with vastly smoother motions, and proved practical across 144 real lettuce harvesting attempts in a greenhouse.
sections.details:
### 3.1 & 3.2 Experimental Setup and Evaluation Protocol
Experiments were conducted in three phases: simulation ablation (200 targets), physical control benchmark (150 targets), and greenhouse harvesting trials (144 heads). In the physical benchmark, PSA-PPO was compared with three representative motion planning baselines (Cartesian+TOTG, RRTConnect, and RRT*) on identical targets, evaluating reaching success, endpoint error, and end-effector acceleration/jerk (RMS jerk) over the final 22 cm approach segment.

### 3.3.1 Simulation Ablation
Ablating the safety terms revealed that removing path-safety rewards dropped the strict success rate from 92.0% to 63.5%, causing dangerous breaches up to 54.3 mm below the baseline plane. Interestingly, removing the side-corridor term improved final endpoint accuracy to 25.3 mm (compared to 32.3 mm for PSA-PPO), yet strict success dropped to 73.0% due to hazardous paths along the way. This highlights that optimizing solely for target endpoint accuracy fails to produce safe harvesting motions.

### 3.3.2 Physical Robot Comparison with Classical Planners
In the 150-target physical UR10e benchmark, PSA-PPO achieved the highest reaching rate of 94.7% (RRTConnect: 88.0%, Cartesian+TOTG: 86.0%, RRT*: 80.0%). While classical planners showed superior terminal positioning accuracy (around 1 mm), PSA-PPO's error of 9.78 mm stayed well within the 20 mm tolerance. Motion smoothness was particularly striking: RMS jerk in the final approach dropped by 73.0% compared to Cartesian+TOTG, 72.1% compared to RRTConnect, and 39.8% compared to RRT*. The arm reached the target quietly without abrupt joint kicks.

### 3.3.3 End-to-End Harvesting Performance in a Greenhouse
In 144 full greenhouse trials from vision detection to cutting and collection, PSA-PPO achieved a 94.4% target-reaching rate (136/144 heads), an 86.1% cut success rate (124 heads), and a 75.0% crate-delivery success rate (108 heads). Most post-reach failures stemmed from physical grasping issues, such as blade jamming or drops during transport, confirming that the learned motion control itself is remarkably robust.

sections.heading: Takeaway: A New Relationship Between Geometric Planning and Learned Control in Harvesting
sections.summary: PSA-PPO proves that a reinforcement learning policy trained purely in simulation can execute safely and smoothly on real hardware in confined hydroponic environments. It clarifies the complementary strengths of geometric planners and RL controllers, charting a clear course for practical harvesting automation.
sections.details:
This study demonstrates that simulation-trained reinforcement learning (PSA-PPO) can operate with high reliability on physical hardware in the constrained task of hydroponic lettuce harvesting. A key takeaway is the trade-off between RL and classical planners. While classical planners excel at finding geometric shortest paths and achieving sub-millimeter terminal accuracy, they are prone to singularities, planning failures in tight spaces, and oscillatory motions. In contrast, PSA-PPO exhibits high reaching reliability and drastically reduced dynamic excitation (vibrations and jerk), which are ideal dynamic properties for agricultural robotics.

Looking ahead, promising next steps point toward hybrid architectures: letting classical geometric planners handle global obstacle avoidance, while learned policies like PSA-PPO manage delicate crop-proximal approaches, augmented with contact-force feedback.

sections.heading: Appendix: Training Details and Workspace-Wide Success Distributions
sections.summary: The appendix details PPO hyperparameters, reward weights, formulas for safe start poses, and success/failure spatial distributions across the simulation workspace for each ablation variant.
sections.details:
PSA-PPO training uses standard hyperparameters, including PPO clipping parameter $\epsilon=0.2$, discount factor $\gamma=0.99$, and GAE parameter $\lambda=0.95$. The policy network receives a 42-dimensional input and outputs 6-DoF joint increment actions through an MLP with hidden layers [256, 128, 64].

Examining the 3D maps visualizing outcomes across the workspace (Figure B.2) reveals that PSA-PPO consistently maintains "strict success" (green circles) even at workspace boundaries and extreme elevation differences. Conversely, the model without path-safety (W/o path safety) exhibits widespread "failures due to safety violations" (orange squares) across the entire space. This confirms that failures are not localized to specific difficult regions, but reflect a breakdown in overall trajectory management.

captions.F14: Success and failure distributions across the workspace evaluated over 200 simulation targets. While PSA-PPO (top-left) maintains strict success (green circles) across the entire volume, removing the path-safety term (top-right) causes safety-violation failures (orange squares) to proliferate throughout the workspace.

takeaways: Rewarding only terminal target-reaching error causes policies to learn dangerous paths that dip below obstacle planes, making whole-trajectory safety criteria and reward formulation essential.

While reinforcement learning controllers lag behind classical planners in sub-millimeter precision and straight-line tracking, they provide superior target-reaching reliability and dramatic reductions in jerk.

Rather than having a single policy solve the entire trajectory, separating target-dependent coarse pre-positioning from the final 20 cm crop-proximal approach drastically improves Sim-to-Real success rates.

Across the full harvesting system, once motion-planning reaching rates exceed 94%, the real bottleneck shifts away from motion control to physical interactions like blade cutting and grasping retention.
limitations: Although termed 'Path-Safe,' the design relies on tool and wrist height clearance thresholds and corridor bounds; it does not provide strict, mathematically proven collision-avoidance guarantees for the entire greenhouse or unforeseen obstacles.
The evaluated policy is based on a single simulation training checkpoint, without assessing variance across multiple random seeds (retraining robustness).

The physical comparison with classical planners was limited to the target-reaching benchmark; direct head-to-head comparisons against classical planners were not conducted during end-to-end vision-guided greenhouse harvesting.
